questions.q: Define Visible Transmittance (VT) or VLT.
o: The total percentage of light reflected by the glass surface.
The amount of visible light that passes through a glazing system.
The ratio of solar heat gain through the glass.
The amount of infrared radiation blocked by a glazing system.
questions.n: VT specifically measures the optical property of glass to transmit visible light.

questions.q: How does a higher VT affect interior environments?
o: It decreases the glare index significantly.
It increases the U-value of the room.
It reduces the need for mechanical ventilation.
questions.n: Higher transmittance allows more photons in the visible spectrum to enter the space.

questions.q: What is the energy benefit of designing for high VT?
o: It can offset or lessen the need for electric lighting.
It improves the power factor of the building.
It increases the R-value of the exterior walls.
It eliminates the need for any artificial cooling.
questions.n: More natural light reduces the runtime and intensity of electrical luminaires.

questions.q: What is the VT of 90% uncoated water-white clear glass?
questions.n: Uncoated water-white glass is highly transparent, allowing 90% of light through.

questions.q: What is the typical VT for heavily tinted glass?
questions.n: Heavily tinted glass is designed to block the majority of visible light.

questions.q: What is the recommended VT range for buildings in the Philippines?
questions.n: This range is considered optimal for balancing daylighting and solar control in the Philippines.

questions.q: What is the VLT requirement if the WWR is 20%?
questions.n: At a low WWR of 20%, a higher VLT is permitted/required to ensure enough light enters.

questions.q: What is the VLT requirement if the WWR is 60%?
questions.n: For a 60% WWR, the VLT requirement drops to 0.50 to control light and heat.

questions.q: What is the VLT for a WWR of 10%?
questions.n: A 10% WWR allows for a high VLT of 0.8 to compensate for small window area.

questions.q: What is the VLT for a WWR of 50%?
questions.n: A 50% WWR specifies a VLT of 0.55.

questions.q: Define Window-to-Wall Ratio (WWR).
o: The ratio of transparent glass to opaque glass.
The volume of windows compared to the volume of the building.
The ratio of window height to total wall height.
The ratio of the total net glazing area to the total gross exterior wall area.
questions.n: This correctly identifies the relationship between glass area and the overall envelope area.

questions.q: If WWR is 90%, what is the VLT?
questions.n: For nearly full-glass facades (90% WWR), the VLT is restricted to 0.35.

questions.q: If WWR is 20%, what is the SHGC?
questions.n: For a 20% WWR, the maximum SHGC allowed is 0.7.

questions.q: If WWR is 80%, what is the VLT?
questions.n: An 80% WWR requires a VLT of 0.40.

questions.q: Why does a WWR of 90% require a lower VLT than a WWR of 10%?
o: Because lower VLT glass is more expensive and fits high-budget 90% glass buildings.
To prevent excessive glare and solar heat gain from the large glass surface area.
To increase the privacy of the building occupants.
Because 90% WWR buildings have stronger structural requirements.
questions.n: Large glass areas admit massive amounts of energy; lowering VLT helps mitigate these effects.

questions.q: If WWR is 60%, what is the SHGC?
questions.n: For a 60% WWR, the SHGC requirement is 0.37.

questions.q: True or False: Proper daylighting design only depends on the VT value.
o: True; if the VT is high, the daylighting is automatically successful.
False; it also requires proper architectural integration to offset electric lighting.
questions.n: Good daylighting needs sensors and design to ensure lights are actually turned off when not needed.

questions.q: What does OTTV stand for?
questions.n: OTTV is the standard term for assessing building envelope heat gain.

questions.q: What does OTTV measure?
o: The amount of heat generated by occupants inside.
The average heat gain into a building through its envelope (walls and windows).
The amount of electricity used by the HVAC system.
The wind pressure exerted on the building exterior.
questions.n: OTTV quantifies the thermal performance of the vertical building skin.

questions.q: What is the maximum permissible OTTV in the Philippines?
questions.n: Philippine standards mandate that the OTTV must not exceed 45 Watts per square meter.

questions.q: What does LPD stand for?
questions.n: LPD is the metric for lighting energy efficiency per unit area.

questions.q: How is LPD calculated?
o: Total lumens divided by the number of fixtures.
Total lighting power (Watts) divided by the total floor area (sqm).
The wattage of one bulb divided by the room height.
Total electricity cost divided by the total floor area.
questions.n: LPD is expressed as W/sqm, relating total wattage to area.

questions.q: What does EER stand for?
questions.n: EER is a standard term for cooling equipment efficiency.

questions.q: What does EEF stand for?
questions.n: EEF is the correct term for the factor used on energy guide labels in the Philippines.

questions.q: Which ratio is commonly used on Philippine energy labels for air conditioners?
questions.n: Philippine energy labels (yellow tags) explicitly display the Energy Efficiency Factor.

questions.q: In cooling equipment, does a higher EER indicate better or worse efficiency?
o: It indicates the unit has a higher noise level.
Efficiency remains the same; it only indicates higher power consumption.
questions.n: A higher ratio means the unit provides more cooling per watt of electricity.

questions.q: How does LPD relate to the building’s cooling load?
o: Higher LPD reduces the cooling load.
Lower LPD increases the cooling load by requiring more fans.
LPD and cooling load are completely independent.
Lower LPD reduces internal heat gain, which lessens the cooling load.
questions.n: Reducing the energy used for lights reduces the heat they emit, saving HVAC energy.

questions.q: If a building exceeds 45 W/sqm OTTV, what is the most effective way to lower it?
o: Decrease the WWR, lower the SHGC, or improve wall insulation (R-value).
Increase the WWR to improve ventilation.
Paint the building a darker color to absorb light.
questions.n: These actions reduce the heat entering through the windows and walls.

questions.q: What glazing type provides the best balance of high VT and low SHGC for the tropics?
questions.n: This glass allows visible light while blocking infrared (heat) radiation.

questions.q: What is the VLT for a WWR of 90%?
questions.n: For the highest glass ratio (90%), the VLT is restricted to its lowest level: 0.35.
